paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: At the beginning of the 20th century, American grocery stores offered full service: customers asked clerks behind counters for the items they wanted, and the clerks wrapped them. To save time, customers could have delivery boys take their shopping lists to a store, or deliver the lists themselves, then return later to pay for the goods. Grocery stores generally stocked only one brand of each item. Early chains such as A&P, although full-service, made shopping time-consuming and inefficient.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Born in Virginia, Clarence Saunders left school at fourteen in 1895 and began work as a grocery clerk. While working, he noticed how inefficient the shopping process was. In an era without computers, the system was cumbersome and wasted considerable time and money. With enthusiasm and imagination, Saunders proposed an unprecedented solution: consumers would serve themselves, an idea that could revolutionise the entire industry.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In 1902, Saunders moved to Memphis to put his idea into practice by establishing a wholesale grocery cooperative. He divided his new store into three areas. A ‘front lobby’ served as both entrance and exit and contained the checkouts. A ‘sales department’ allowed customers to walk along aisles and select their own groceries. Clerks no longer retrieved every item; instead, neatly arranged aisles and shelves displayed the goods and allowed shoppers to browse. From a gallery above the sales department, supervisors could observe customers without disturbing them. A third area, the ‘stockroom’, contained large refrigerators for keeping products fresh and was open only to staff. The new layout accommodated more customers at once and contributed to phenomena that had previously been unimaginable, including impulse buying and, later, the supermarket.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: On 6 September 1916, Saunders launched the self-service revolution in the United States by opening the first Piggly Wiggly at 79 Jefferson Street in Memphis, Tennessee. The store featured a turnstile at its entrance. Unlike customers in conventional groceries, Piggly Wiggly shoppers selected goods from shelves and paid for the items themselves. They were not at the mercy of staff but could roam freely, inspect products and choose what they needed. Items were clearly priced, and no one pressured customers to buy unwanted goods. The greatest benefit was lower prices. ‘It is good for both the consumer and retailer because it cuts costs,’ noted George T. Haley, a professor at the University of New Haven and director of the Centre for International Industry Competitiveness. ‘If you look at how grocery stores operated before Piggly Wiggly and Alpha Beta, you find that a great many workers were involved, and labour is a major expense.’ Chains such as Piggly Wiggly therefore cut unnecessary costs.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Piggly Wiggly and other self-service stores rapidly gained popularity. Saunders opened nine Memphis branches in the first year, immediately applied for a patent on the self-service concept and began franchising the stores. Through self-service and franchising, the chain grew to nearly 1,300 locations by 1923. Piggly Wiggly sold $100 million in groceries—equivalent to about $1.3 billion today—and became the nation’s third-largest grocery retailer. It was listed on the New York Stock Exchange, where its share price doubled between late 1922 and March 1923. Saunders contributed greatly to the design and layout of grocery stores and even invented the turnstile to keep customers moving smoothly through the entrance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Clarence Saunders died in 1953, leaving a lasting legacy symbolised chiefly by Piggly Wiggly, whose model spread widely and endured.

questionGroups.text:
Questions 1–5
Reading Passage 1 has six paragraphs, A–F.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A–F, in Boxes 1–5 on your answer sheet.
NB You may use any letter more than once.
1 ____________ layout of Clarence Saunders’ store
2 ____________ a reference to a reduction by chain stores in labour costs
3 ____________ how Clarence Saunders implemented his idea
4 ____________ how people used to shop before Clarence Saunders’ stores opened
5 ____________ a description of the economic success generated by Saunders’s stores

Questions 6–10
Complete the sentences below.
Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in Boxes 6–10 on your answer sheet.
Clarence Saunders’s first job in a grocery store was as 6 _________________.
In Saunders’s store, customers paid for goods in the 7 _________________.
Customers were under surveillance while shopping in the 8 _________________.
Another area was called the ‘9 _________________’ and was accessible only to staff.
In Saunders’s design, much of the work was done by the 10 _________________.

Questions 11–13
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in Boxes 11–13 on your answer sheet.


11 Why did Clarence Saunders want to improve grocery stores?
  A He wanted to transfer business to retailing.
  B He thought it was profitable.
  C He thought this would make customers’ lives more convenient.
  D He wanted to create a new shop by himself.


12 The Piggly Wiggly store was
  A located in Virginia.
  B characterised primarily by self-service.
  C initially very unpopular with customers.
  D expected to have a poor future.


13 Today, Clarence Saunders is chiefly remembered for
  A the opening of a fully automatic store near his first store.
  B the popularity of his Piggly Wiggly store at the time.
  C his association with Piggly Wiggly stores.
  D having his name printed alongside that of his famous store.
